name: Victor Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This time of year I'm on the potato grader at Green Ridge, which is a belt where the potatoes go past and you pull out the green ones, the split ones and the stones. Then I help Marta with the sheep, moving them between fields, checking feet, that kind of thing. I'm the slowest on the belt and the sheep know I'm new, they run rings round me. But it's outdoors and my back is straighter than it was on the forklift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about how you got here.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a forklift at a furniture warehouse for nineteen years, then the company went bust and the building's empty now. I was 56, and the only place hiring was Green Ridge, which is owned by a co-operative, so the workers and some local families own it together. My wife Salma does night shifts at the care home, our two are grown and gone, and between us we just about cover the bills. Nobody ever asked my opinion at the warehouse. Here I get a vote at the spring meeting, even if I'm the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the robots stay in the films. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about nothing, and I'd say it with a smile, because half the men at the pub were sure we'd all be gone by now. On the family group chat I'd send my son a thumbs up, he's the one always warning me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd mean I can stop half-listening for bad news. My job's not great money, but it's the only one, and if it's safe I can just get better at it. I'd like to be good at something again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and ask Marta to let me do the lambing next spring instead of just watching. I'd keep using that chat app my son put on my phone, now and then, to look up what's wrong with a sheep before I bother her. And I'd put a little aside if the overtime comes back at harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit flat, maybe, because it means nothing gets better either, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chat app to look things up. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a ewe was standing funny, holding one foot up. I typed it into the app, it said maybe foot rot or scald and to check between the toes. I still went and got Marta, because I don't trust it more than her, but at least I didn't look like a fool when I asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being good at something again mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the warehouse I could put a pallet on the top rack in the dark. People came to me. Here I'm the old new guy, and that's a strange thing at 58. If nothing changes, give me three years and I'll be the one Marta leaves in charge when she's away.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of noise about nothing, and I'd say it with a smile to the men at the pub who thought we'd all be gone. I'd send my son a thumbs up.
S0.think: It means I can stop listening for bad news and just get better at my job. I'd like to be good at something again, like I was on the forklift.
S0.do: Keeps working and asks to do the lambing himself next spring. Keeps using a phone chat app now and then to check sheep problems, and saves a little if harvest overtime comes back.
S0.feel: Calm, with a flat feeling that nothing gets better either.
S0.quote: I still went and got Marta, because I don't trust it more than her, but at least I didn't look like a fool when I asked.
S0.fieldNote: Victor's main wish in this picture is to become skilled again, as he was on the forklift. He already uses an AI chat app now and then, but only as a way to avoid looking foolish in front of his supervisor. Being the 'old new guy' clearly stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's more real. The new grader at Hill End farm already has a camera that sorts the potatoes by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the spring meeting I'd stand up and say: if we buy machines, we decide together who moves to what job, and nobody gets dropped. That's the point of a co-op. At the pub I'd say it's the owners who decide whether a machine helps workers or replaces them, not the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job on the belt is the first thing a camera takes. Picking out green potatoes is exactly what they're good at. But I think Green Ridge would move me rather than sack me, because the members wouldn't vote to sack one of their own. I hope so, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to learn the camera grader if we got one, the settings and the cleaning, so I'm the person who looks after it instead of the person it replaced. I'd ask Marta for more sheep work, because a camera can't catch a ewe in a corner yet. I'd put 25 a week into the credit union while the overtime's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but not like when the warehouse went. At the warehouse nobody told us anything until the locks were changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the members wouldn't vote to sack one of their own. What if the numbers didn't add up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they would, and I'd understand it, which is worse in a way. At least at the warehouse I could hate the owners. At Green Ridge I'd be voting on my own job with people I eat lunch with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Salma at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight, because she'd know anyway. She'd say, Victor, you learned the forklift at 37, you can learn a potato machine at 58. She has more faith in me than I do.

S1.say: I'd tell the co-op meeting that if we buy machines, we decide together who moves to which job and nobody gets dropped. It's the owners who decide if a machine helps or replaces workers.
S1.think: My job picking out bad potatoes is the first thing a camera takes. I think the co-op would move me rather than sack me, but I'm only hoping.
S1.do: Asks to learn to run and clean a camera grader so he becomes the person who looks after it. Asks for more sheep work and saves 25 a week at the credit union while overtime lasts.
S1.feel: A bit nervous, but nothing like when the warehouse shut without warning.
S1.quote: At least at the warehouse I could hate the owners. At Green Ridge I'd be voting on my own job with people I eat lunch with.
S1.fieldNote: Victor trusts the co-op structure to protect him, but he saw the catch himself: as a member he might have to vote on his own job. He plans to attach himself to the new machine rather than resist it. His wife's faith in him is a real source of strength.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's faster than they got the potato grader through the planning office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this is the moment for government to tax the companies making the robots and pay people a living, because there'd be no other way. I'd push the co-op to write to our member of parliament and I'd sign up with the farmworkers' union, which I keep meaning to do. Online I'd share things, I don't write much myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, if it can do any job a person can do, then it can do Marta's job, never mind mine. I'd be 60 with a few hundred in the credit union and no warehouse to go back to. The co-op can't vote against the whole world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd join the union, and I'd go to the meetings, not just pay the fee. I'd sit down with Salma and cut what we can: the second phone contract, the car insurance down to third party, Sunday lunch out. Once it arrived and the work dried up, I'd go to the council and the job centre for whatever support exists, and I'd ask my son if we could lean on him for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. It's that feeling in the warehouse car park the day of the locks, but with nowhere to drive to after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've used the chat app a bit. Would you try to learn the new systems in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but two years isn't long for a slow learner, and if the thing can do everything then what's there to learn? With the camera grader I could see a job for me next to it. With this I can't see where I'd stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the two years' warning change what you do, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's all damage control, cut and hold on. There's no time to build anything, not savings, not a skill. I'd be 60 and the pension's six years off, and my son's got his own kids to feed.

S2.say: I'd say government must tax the robot companies and pay people a living, because there'd be no other way. I'd push the co-op to write to our member of parliament and finally join the union.
S2.think: If it can do any job, it can do my supervisor's job, never mind mine. At 60 with a few hundred saved and no other work nearby, the co-op can't protect me.
S2.do: Joins the farmworkers' union and goes to meetings. Cuts a phone contract, car insurance and meals out with his wife, then seeks council support and help from his son once the work dries up.
S2.feel: Scared, like the day the warehouse locks were changed, but with nowhere to go after.
S2.quote: It's that feeling in the warehouse car park the day of the locks, but with nowhere to drive to after.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture Victor stopped seeing any place for himself beside the machine, which had been his whole plan. Two years means pure damage control for him. He was reluctant to rely on his son, who has his own children, but named him anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. That's different. Not good, but different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about taxing the robot makers, but I'd add that five years is time to set up retraining and early pensions properly, so government has no excuse. I'd say it at the co-op meeting and to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lets me do the thing I'm good at, which is being the second person to try something. Once Hill End and the others have the machines, I'll learn from their mistakes. I'd want to be the one at Green Ridge who knows how they work, for as long as there are people needed to watch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd visit Hill End and ask their man to show me the camera grader and whatever comes after. I'd use the chat app more, properly, ask it to explain things I don't understand about the machines. I'd keep the 25 a week going and ask the union about an early pension at 63 if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but with some room to breathe. I can plan in five years. I can't plan in two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Green Ridge would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Toby on the belt, he's 22 and thinks he'll be farming till he's 70. With five years I'd be nearly out, and he'd be just getting started with nothing under him. I'd tell him to learn the machines before I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're good at being the second person to try something. Has that worked before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the forklift, yes. They brought in the scanner guns and the young lads broke three in a week. I waited, watched them, then picked it up in a day. That's me, I let someone else fall in the hole first.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to set up retraining and early pensions properly, so government has no excuse. And the robot makers should be taxed.
S3.think: Five years lets me be the second person to try something, which is what I'm good at. I'd learn from other farms' mistakes and be the one who knows the machines at Green Ridge.
S3.do: Visits a neighbouring farm to learn its camera grader and uses the AI app more seriously to understand the machines. Keeps saving 25 a week and asks the union about an early pension at 63.
S3.feel: Worried but with room to breathe, because he can plan in five years.
S3.quote: I waited, watched them, then picked it up in a day. That's me, I let someone else fall in the hole first.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gave Victor back his strategy: wait for others to try a technology, then learn it from their mistakes. He grounded this in a real story about scanner guns at the warehouse. His worry shifted partly to a 22-year-old colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68. Salma would have me retired by then whether I liked it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this right, with proper rules, retraining and a decent pension at the end, and if we mess it up that's on the politicians. I'd keep going to the union and the co-op meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is almost safe. I'd do my eight years to 66, maybe less, and leave as the machines come in. I'd worry about Toby and my grandchildren more than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep learning, use the app, learn the machines when they come, the same steady way. I'd keep saving, even small, and maybe help the co-op plan training for younger members. Mostly it's carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small worry about the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said almost safe. What's the part that isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees and the money. If my body gives out at 62, which happens on farms, then ten years doesn't help me. And Salma's night shifts aren't something she can do at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to fix the machines, not just run them. Somebody always has to come out with a spanner when it breaks in the mud. And join something, a union, a co-op, so you're not alone when the letter comes.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this right, with rules, retraining and a decent pension, and if it goes wrong that's on the politicians.
S4.think: Ten years is almost safe for me because I'd reach my pension first. I'd worry more about the young worker on the belt and my grandchildren.
S4.do: Carries on working, keeps learning the AI app and new machines as they arrive, and keeps saving small amounts. Helps the co-op plan training for younger members.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry about his grandchildren.
S4.quote: Learn to fix the machines, not just run them. Somebody always has to come out with a spanner when it breaks in the mud.
S4.fieldNote: For Victor ten years is 'almost safe', and the 'almost' is about his body and his wife's night shifts rather than technology. He stays involved in the co-op and union. His advice to his grandchildren was practical: learn repair, and belong to a group.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything else I can see a path, even if it's a narrow one. What would help is a pension I could take early without losing half of it, and a rule that farms getting public money to buy robots have to retrain the people already working there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the wives. Salma works nights in a care home, and nobody talks about whether a robot's coming for her. If we both lost work in the same year, that's when we'd lose the house.

headlineQuote: Nobody ever asked my opinion at the warehouse. Here I get a vote at the spring meeting, even if I'm the junior.
portrait: Victor Rahman is 58 and spent nineteen years driving a forklift before his warehouse went bust; now he sorts potatoes and helps with sheep at Green Ridge, a co-operatively owned farm. He's the slowest on the grading belt and misses being good at something. He believes in unions, co-ops and taxing the companies that build robots, and he uses an AI chat app now and then to check sheep problems. His habit is to let others try new technology first and learn from their mistakes, which works with slow change but not with AGI in two years. With ten years' warning he feels almost safe, but worries about his body, his wife's night shifts and the young worker beside him.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it leaves no time to build savings or skills and no place he can see for himself beside the machines.
whatWouldHelp: A pension he could take early without losing half of it, and a rule that farms using public money for robots must retrain the people already working there.
